title: Quasiparticle interference as a tool to study quantum materials
authors: Luke C. Rhodes, Yuhki Kohsaka, Tetsuo Hanaguri, Carolina de Almeida Marques, Peter Wahl
abstract: To understand the properties of quantum materials a detailed knowledge of the material's low energy electronic structure is key. Details of the electronic structure drive the ground state through electronic instabilities, electronic correlation effects, new electronic orders or just the absence of electronic states near the Fermi energy - making a realistic and detailed understanding crucial to be able to control and design properties of quantum materials. The past 25 years have seen a significant improvement in experimental techniques to observe the true electronic structure, in particular in techniques such as Angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) where energy resolutions of 2meV are routinely achievable now, which however is limited to zero magnetic field and only provides information about the occupied states. Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) achieves a significantly better energy resolution <100$μ$eV and can operate at temperatures well below 50mK and in magnetic fields. While per se a real-space technique, by imaging quasiparticle interference (QPI) STM can also provide information about the electronic structure. This technique has been used over the past decades to study a wide range of quantum materials to understand correlated electron behaviour. Recent theoretical progress now enables routine modelling of QPI, a key requirement to interpret the complex data. Here, we review the principles of QPI, its origin, experimental detection, and the physical insight gained from the study of QPI and possible future directions for this technique.
summary: This review details Quasiparticle Interference (QPI) as a vital experimental technique for probing the low-energy electronic structure of quantum materials. By analyzing standing wave patterns observed via STM, researchers can map out momentum-space information related to electron scattering. This methodology has proven invaluable across diverse fields, from topological insulators to unconventional superconductors.
main_problem: Understanding the properties of quantum materials requires detailed knowledge of their low energy electronic structure to enable control and design.
main_result: Quasiparticle interference (QPI) imaging using STM provides a powerful, real-space tool to map out the underlying electronic structure, revealing details about correlations and symmetries in various novel materials.
method: The study reviews QPI principles, which are experimentally detected via Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) by analyzing standing wave modulations in the Local Density of States (LDOS). Theoretical modeling is crucial for interpreting these complex scattering patterns.
model_or_system: The focus is on various quantum materials, including topological insulators, Weyl semimetals, graphene, and unconventional superconductors. The analysis relies on STM measurements of tunneling current/conductance ($g(r, V)$) which are sensitive to the electronic structure via quasiparticle scattering.
key_observables: Standing wave patterns in LDOS modulations; Fourier Transform ($	ilde{g}(q_x, q_y, V)$) revealing momentum-space information (dispersion relations); superconducting gap structures and Fermi arc signatures.
important_parameters: Low energy electronic structure details; temperature regimes down to 50mK; magnetic fields; scattering vectors ($q$).
main_assumptions: The interpretation of QPI data requires advanced theoretical modeling, and experimental measurements must account for artifacts like the setpoint effect or raster scanning distortions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate initial QPI experiments on noble metal surfaces showing standing wave patterns and extracted dispersion relations, alongside diagrams detailing the STM working principle and tunneling current measurement geometry.
paper_structure: The review progresses by first establishing the necessity of electronic structure knowledge. It then details the experimental capabilities of STM/QPI, covering theory (elastic vs. inelastic tunneling), data acquisition ($g(r, V)$), and analysis (Fourier Transform). Finally, it reviews successful applications across diverse quantum materials.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter, the underlying physics involves many-body dynamics and electronic correlations in strongly interacting systems, which shares conceptual overlap with open quantum system descriptions of quasiparticle interactions.
